sources.text: Search this site Embedded Files Aguado iBiomaterials Lab ENGINEERING BIOMATERIALS TO UNDERSTAND SEX DIFFERENCES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE The Aguado iBiomaterials Research Group WELCOME! The Aguado iBiomaterials Research Group develops precision biomaterials as tools to determine how sex, age, and ancestry impact health and disease at multiple length scales . Our current focus is investigat ing how sex chromosome linked genes modulate sex differences in cardiovascular disease progression and treatments . Our long-term goal is to achieve sex and gender equity in our unders tanding of cardiovascular disease and move toward equitable treatments and outcomes. Congratulations to Rayyan Gorashi, Ph.D. Sept 2 , 2026 Congratulations and best wishes to Dr. Rayyan Gorashi, PhD, the first PhD graduate from the Aguado Lab! Dr. Gorashi's research has revealed a novel role for sex chromosomes in regulating sex differences in cellular phenotypes using bioengineered platforms for valve and cardiac fibroblast culture. Her collaborative research has led to an impressive 5 peer reviewed co-authored publications during her time in the lab, including first author publications in Science Advances and the Journal of Materials Chemistry B. Her research has been recognized with the NIH NHLBI R00 Fellowship Supplement, the NIH NHLBI F31 Ruth L. Kirschstein Predoctoral Individual National Research Service Award, the ARCS Foundation Scholarship, the Siebel Scholar Award, the European Molecular Biology Organization Best Poster Prize, and she was also elected to the Edward A. Bouchet Graduate Honor Society launched at Yale University and Howard University. The Aguado Lab can't congratulate and celebrate you enough!! Read More Congratulations to Kimmy Wennerholm , M.S. August 2 7, 2026 Super happy to celebrate Kimberly Wennerholm for defending her MS thesis - 3rd MS alum from the Aguado Lab!! Kimmy came to our lab from Georgia Tech and worked super hard with her mentor Talia Baddour to utilize a collagen-based hydrogel system in her thesis to evaluate male and female aortic valve fibroblast responses to naturally derived matrix cues - a fun departure from our beloved synthetic PEG matrix! Read More Congratulations to Vivian Zheng, M.S. August 17, 2026 Huge congratulations to Vivian Zheng on defending her MS thesis!! Her MS thesis work was focused on understanding how biological sex influences immune cell and cancer stem cell plasticity in the tumor microenvironment during squamous cell carcinoma. Double celebrations are in order, because Vivian was the first co-mentored student between the Aguado Lab and Shiri Gur-Cohen's Lab! Vivian will be moving on to a Research Associate I position in the Hacohen lab at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard Read More Brandon Vogt publishes in Cell Reports July 22, 2026 Vogt et al determined that IGFBP2 levels in serum from female aortic valve stenosis patients causes valve myofibroblast resistance to the inhibitor Evogliptin via mechanosensing pathways - another super cool mechanism determined with our hydrogel cell culture platforms - check it out! Read More Jaden Gilliam joins the lab as a summer rotation student Ju ne 24 , 2026 Jaden Gilliam joins the lab for the summer helping Brandon with his work to characterize the impact of mLOY on anti-fibrotic drug treatment in valvular fibroblasts. Welcome to the Aguado lab Jaden! Mason Faust and Dr. Ash Nguyen publish in Cellular and Molecular Bioengineering June 2 2 , 2026 Faust/Nguyen et al worked to characterize sex-dependent myofibroblast activation on hydrogel biomaterials, and observed sex-dependencies in TGF-b induced activation and SD-208 inhibition. Congratulations on the article featured in the 2026 CMBE Young Innovator Special Issue! Read More Rene Peña and Kati Richter receive the Faculty Award for the UCSD Undergraduate Research Symposium! May 28, 2026 Huge congratulations to Rene Peña and Kati Richter for your well deserved award and for representing the lab and sharing your projects! Talia Baddour publishes in Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology May 28, 2026 Talia et al collected human aortic valve samples over several years to create the first spatial transcriptomics atlas of the human aortic valve, and determined transcriptomic sex differences in valvular interstitial cells and macrophages that promote female-biased valve fibrosis and male-biased valve calcification - so many cool findings in the paper! sources.text: Faculty Profiles Back to Faculty Profiles Brian Aguado Assistant Professor, BENG Biomaterials, tissue engineering, precision medicine, sex differences, cardiovascular disease, immunoengineering The mission of the Aguado iBiomaterials Research Group is to develop "precision biomaterials" that enable the evaluation of a patient’s unique biology to diagnose and treat a variety of health disorders as a function of sex, age, and/or ancestry. Our multidisciplinary team is currently focused on using precision biomaterials as in vitro and in vivo tools to understand sex as a biological variable in cardiovascular disorders, including aortic valve disease and heart failure. We operate at multiple length scales to understand how sex hormones, sex chromosomes, cardiac cells, biochemical/mechanical cues from the tissue microenvironment, and inflammation all contribute to sex differences in cardiovascular diseases. Our efforts will improve our understanding of sexual dimorphisms in health and disease, which represents the next step toward developing more effective sex-specific therapies. LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/brian- aguado -ph-d-1a73242b/ Lab Website: Aguado iBiomaterials Research Group ( https:// aguado .eng.ucsd.edu/ ) Capsule Bio: Dr. Brian Aguado completed his BS degree in Biomechanical Engineering from Stanford University and his MS and PhD in Biomedical Engineering from Northwestern University. He also obtained his certificate in Management for Scientists and Engineers from the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern. He completed his postdoctoral fellowship in Chemical and Biological Engineering at the University of Colorado Boulder. Dr. Aguado has received numerous grants to support his research program, including the NIH K99/R00 Pathway to Independence Award, the American Heart Association Career Development Award, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Science Diversity Leadership Award, the NIH DP2 New Innovator Award, the NSF CAREER Award, and the Women’s Health Access Matters (WHAM) Edge Award. Dr. Aguado is also the recipient of the Society for Biomaterials Young Investigator Award, the American Society of Matrix Biology Young Investigator Award, the Cellular and Molecular Bioengineering (CMBE) Rising Star Award, the CMBE Young Innovator Award, the Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine International Society (TERMIS) Young Investigator Award, and the Great Minds in STEM Most Promising Engineer HENAAC Award. Dr. Aguado also co-founded the non-profit organization LatinXinBME, a grassroots virtual mentoring group of Latinx biomedical engineers dedicated to building a community that supports each other personally and professionally through their careers. For his mentoring and teaching efforts, he was named one of the 100 Most Inspiring Latinx Scientists in America by Cell Press and received the Society for Biomaterials Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Award, the BMES Diversity Award, the ASEE Constituent DEI Award, the ISSCR Public Service Award, the Teacher of the Year Award from the Jacobs School of Engineering, and the GEMINI Faculty Mentor Award from the UCSD Institute for Engineering in Medicine.
